q: Saccharomyces pastorianus, the bottom-fermenting lager yeast, is a hybrid of S. cerevisiae and:
opts: Saccharomyces eubayanus, a cold-tolerant wild species
exp: S. eubayanus was identified in 2011 in Patagonian beech forests and has since been found in Tibet, North America and Ireland; the hybrid it forms with ale yeast inherited cold tolerance from one parent and fermentation vigour from the other. That is why lager ferments cleanly at 8-12C, throws few esters and finishes with a long cold conditioning. It also ferments melibiose, which ale yeast generally cannot — the classic laboratory distinction. The wider point for the exam: lager is a young style precisely because it needed both cold cellars and an accidental hybridisation to exist at all.

q: Name the compound behind 'skunked' beer, the reaction that makes it, and the two ways a brewer prevents it in pale glass.
accept: mbt from riboflavin cleaving iso alpha acids prevented by brown glass or reduced hop extracts
lightstruck thiol formed by light acting on riboflavin and isohumulones use brown glass or tetra hop acids
skunk thiol made by light on the hop bitter acids brown glass or modified hop extracts
ans: 3-methyl-2-butene-1-thiol, MBT. Light in the near-UV and blue range — daylight and fluorescent tubes, not heat — excites riboflavin from the malt, which cleaves the side chain off the hop iso-alpha acids; the fragment combines with a sulfur radical to give a thiol perceptible at parts per trillion. Prevention: brown glass, which blocks the relevant wavelengths where green and clear glass barely do; or hopping with reduced hop extracts — tetrahydro- or rho-iso-alpha acids — whose bonds cannot be cleaved this way, which is how clear-bottled beers survive.
exp: This is a packaging and display fault, not an age or temperature fault, and the distinction is the point: a green-bottled pilsner can skunk in minutes on a sunlit terrace or under a shop's fluorescents, while a brown-bottled one on the same shelf will not. Calling it correctly tells the supplier what to fix. Cans and kegs are immune by construction, which is a real argument for canned hoppy beer.

q: Bavarian Weissbier's banana and clove: name the compound behind each and the process choice that dials it up.
accept: isoamyl acetate for banana and 4-vinyl guaiacol for clove
banana ester isoamyl acetate clove phenol from decarboxylation of ferulic acid
warm open ferment raises the banana ester a ferulic acid rest raises the clove phenol
ans: Banana is isoamyl acetate, an ester: warmer fermentation, under-pitching, low aeration and open, unpressurised vessels raise it, while fermenting under pressure suppresses ester formation. Clove is 4-vinyl guaiacol, a phenol produced when a POF-positive (phenolic off-flavour) Weissbier yeast decarboxylates ferulic acid released from the malt; a ferulic acid rest around 43-45C in the mash liberates more precursor and pushes the clove higher. House style is decided by which of the two the brewer chases.
exp: Both compounds come from the yeast strain first and the process second, which is why Weissbier yeast is jealously guarded and why the same strain in a different brewery makes a recognisably different beer. Note the inversion: German lager yeast is selected to be POF-negative precisely so that 4-vinyl guaiacol never appears, where in Weissbier and much of Belgium it is the signature. Wheat's contribution is protein and mouthfeel plus haze, not the aroma everyone credits it with.

q: Name three French cider or perry AOCs and the region of each.
accept: pays d auge cornouaille cotentin and poire domfront
cidre pays d auge in normandy and cidre cornouaille in brittany
pays d auge cornouaille and domfront for perry
ans: Cidre Pays d'Auge (Normandy, 1996), Cidre Cornouaille (Brittany, 1996), Cidre Cotentin (Normandy, 2016), and for perry, Poire Domfront (the Domfrontais in Normandy, 2002, built on the Plant de Blanc pear).
exp: The appellations exist to separate real cider from the industrial category. They require whole-fruit pressing from listed cider varieties, no added sugar, no concentrate, and carbonation generated by the fruit's own residual sugar in bottle or tank rather than injected — which is exactly the ground on which a somm defends a cider's place next to wine. Pays d'Auge is bittersweet, keeved, richly bitter and often bottle-fermented; Cornouaille is slower and more tannic; Domfront demands a majority of Plant de Blanc from standard orchards whose trees take a generation to crop, which is why perry is the rarer and harder craft.
